messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Vignette:
Kwame is a 47-year-old African American man who now works as a park ranger, a job he once chose because being outdoors had always felt steadying and familiar. Before coming to treatment, he had gone years without saying much about the period when, as a civilian caught in a war zone, that same kind of landscape became inseparable from terror. When he describes the event, he does not give it in a smooth sequence. What stands out instead are a few sharp moments: dry brush catching fire, the sudden spread of flames across open ground, the confusion of people running in different directions, and the realization that no one nearby was in control. He remembers being with others who did not get out. He did. What has stayed with him most is not only the fear, but the fact that in those moments he acted in ways he now feels ashamed of, making choices under pressure that he believes went against the man he thought himself to be.

In the months after he reached safety, Kwame found that ordinary situations took on the feeling of danger. Fire was the most obvious. Even a controlled campfire or the sight of flames in a fire ring at work could stop him in place. He would feel his body tighten before he had fully registered what he was seeing. Nature itself became complicated. As a ranger, he spends his days in wooded areas, open trails, and dry stretches of land, and there are certain combinations of heat, brush, and light that feel too close to where it happened. On those days he becomes watchful and tense, scanning the environment as if something is about to erupt. He says he cannot relax even when he knows, logically, that he is in a safe park in the United States. His body does not seem to accept that reassurance.

Other moments catch him by surprise. If a supervisor corrects him over the radio or points out a mistake, his reaction is immediate and disproportionate even to himself. What lands on someone else as routine feedback feels to him like a threat, as if criticism means he has failed in some fundamental, dangerous way. He becomes flooded with the old conviction that he made the wrong choices when it mattered most. He had come to believe that surviving when others did not says something damning about him. The guilt is not abstract. It appears in the way he talks about those who died and then stops short when the conversation gets too close to why he lived. He is certain, at those times, that he does not belong among people whose lives remained ordinary.

Over time, his world narrowed. Although his work requires contact with colleagues and the public, outside of work he cut off nearly all contact with friends and family. He stopped returning calls and ignored messages until eventually people reached out less. Being with others intensified his sense of being set apart, and solitude came to feel simpler, even as it made his life smaller. He also began avoiding military and police uniforms, as well as visible weapons. If law enforcement officers were present in the park, he would take a different route or keep his distance. He could not explain it in a way that felt sufficient to others; he only knew that the sight of uniforms immediately made him feel on edge and trapped in a state of expectation.

His nights have become one of the clearest measures of how little peace he feels. He struggles to fall asleep and wakes easily. Delays unsettle him in the same way. If a coworker is late returning from a trail check, if a routine radio response takes longer than expected, if a vehicle is overdue, his mind leaps quickly to catastrophe. He does not experience these thoughts as excessive in the moment; he feels as though he is recognizing danger before other people do. To blunt the tension, he has increasingly relied on alcohol and whatever medication or drugs are available to him, especially in the evenings, telling himself he needs something to quiet down enough to sleep.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a recent incident at work. During a dry-weather patrol, he caught sight of flames from a permitted burn in a nearby area, and around the same time a supervisor corrected him sharply for failing to respond promptly on the radio. He found himself unable to settle for the rest of the shift, certain something terrible was unfolding because another ranger was delayed returning. Afterward he went home, drank heavily, and realized how completely alone his life had become. He comes to treatment frightened by how cut off he is, by how quickly ordinary moments turn into danger in his mind, and by the possibility that the worst thing about what happened is what it revealed about him. At the same time, he is hoping—carefully, without much confidence—that he might find a way to live in the outdoors again without feeling that the past is waiting for him there.
